passage:
Dear Naveen Bhai,
You asked on the phone why I sound 'off'. I don't really know how to explain it. Nothing's wrong. I've got the boys, I've got my games, cricket on Sundays, exams went fine. But everything feels flat, like a cold drink with no fizz. I open a game and close it after five minutes. The boys plan something and I go, but I'm sort of watching from outside.
It's not sad exactly. It's more like, what's the point of any of it? I want something that matters, and I don't know what that is.
Remember when you took me to help at the flood relief camp? That's the last time I felt properly awake.
Farhan

qa.a: A cold drink with no fizz.

qa.q: What does Farhan seem to be missing, judging by the relief camp memory?
qa.a: Farhan seems to miss a sense of purpose; being useful at the relief camp made Farhan feel properly awake.

qa.a: Naveen Bhai could help Farhan find regular volunteering or a project that feels meaningful, and if the flatness gets heavier or lasts, suggest talking to a parent or school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Naveen Bhai read this email?
qa.a: Naveen Bhai might be relieved Farhan isn't in trouble but also concerned, and touched that the camp they shared still means so much.

passage: You want to know why I skipped the party, Ankita? Honestly? I didn't feel like anything. Not sad, just… nothing. I had the new racing game Dad bought, I finished it in two days, and then I sat there holding the controller like, now what? Everyone was posting from the party and I was scrolling, and it all looked like a picture of fun, not actual fun. I'm Francis, I'm supposed to be the one who's up for everything, right? But lately it's like someone turned the colour down. Last week in the library I found this book about people building a school in a desert, and I read it till the lights went off. That's the only time I forgot to be bored. Maybe I don't need more stuff to do. Maybe I need something that means something.

qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What does Francis mean by "a picture of fun, not actual fun"?
qa.a: Francis sees the party as entertainment that looks good but feels empty, because nothing seems to matter right now.

qa.q: The library book was a turning point. What could Francis choose to do with that clue?
qa.a: Francis could look for a real project with a purpose, like volunteering, and talk to a trusted adult if the flatness keeps going.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing this?
qa.a: Ankita may be surprised, since Francis is usually up for everything, and glad that Francis trusted Ankita enough to explain.

passage: My sister Vasudha is fifteen, and something's changed this summer. I'm Parul, the older one, home from college. She's got everything she asked for: the phone, the gaming headset, her friends on call every evening. But she lies on her bed with the headset round her neck, not playing. When her friends call, she says 'hmm' and 'okay' and 'whatever.' Yesterday I asked if she wanted to go for pani puri, her favourite, and she said, 'What's the point? It'll just be pani puri.' I don't know what's going on in her head. She doesn't seem sad, exactly. More like she's waiting for something that isn't games or snacks. Tonight I'm asking if she wants to help me at the animal shelter on Saturday, and I'll mention it to Mummy too.

qa.a: Pani puri.

passage:
Sunday. Leela's friends dragged her to the new food court. They laughed at a video on Ritika's phone; Leela laughed a second late. The fries tasted of nothing. At home she opened her game and didn't press start.
Wednesday. Kathak class, which she had begged for at ten, felt like counting steps for no reason. "What's the point?" she muttered, and sat out. On the bus she scrolled the same five apps and felt nothing at all.
Saturday. Seema Maasi, visiting, noticed. She didn't ask what was wrong. She said, "I'm painting the anganwadi wall tomorrow. Need hands." Leela went, mostly to get out of the house. By noon she was painting a giant tortoise while four-year-olds shouted ideas at her. On the way home she realised she hadn't checked her phone once. "Can I come next week?"

qa.q: What did Leela paint on the anganwadi wall?
qa.a: A giant tortoise, while four-year-olds shouted ideas at her.

qa.q: What does Leela's muttering "What's the point?" suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests she feels flat and empty, with nothing seeming worth doing, even things she once loved.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Leela, and why did it help?
qa.a: Going to paint the anganwadi wall with Seema Maasi gave her something that mattered to others, which the games and outings hadn't.

qa.q: What might Seema Maasi have been thinking when she offered the painting job instead of asking what was wrong?
qa.a: She may have sensed Leela needed something meaningful to do more than questions, and chose a gentle way in.

grounding: A teen with friends and games feels flat until a task with real meaning stirs her.

passage:
Preeti, you keep saying everything is boring and nothing matters. Your Vijay Nana knows that feeling. I was sixteen in 1979. I had a cricket bat, a transistor radio, friends at every corner of the mohalla. And one summer, none of it tasted of anything. I'd stand in the field at cricket thinking, why? I'd switch off the radio halfway through my favourite song. My mother thought I was ill. I wasn't sad, exactly. I was empty, like a bucket with a hole in it.
Then our headmaster asked a few of us to teach the small children of the construction workers in the evenings. Letters, counting. I went because I had nothing better to do. The first time a little girl read a word on her own, something moved in my chest. It wasn't fun, beta. It was more than fun. It mattered.
And if the empty feeling stays heavy, you tell your mother or me. We'll find help together.

qa.q: What did young Vijay own that summer?
qa.a: A cricket bat and a transistor radio.

qa.q: How did young Vijay feel that summer, despite having friends and fun things?
qa.a: He felt empty, "like a bucket with a hole in it", not sad exactly, with nothing tempting him.

qa.q: What choice changed things for young Vijay, and what is Nana suggesting for Preeti?
qa.a: Teaching the workers' children gave him meaning; Nana hints Preeti might look for something that matters, and to tell family if the heaviness stays.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel hearing that Nana once felt the same?
qa.a: Preeti might feel less alone and less odd, and more willing to talk about that flat feeling.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage summer of flat emptiness despite friends and games, eased by finding meaning.
